Lemma
[Block-Permutation Collapse]

For a permutation $\chi $ of $\iota _a \sqcup \iota _b$, let \[ D(\chi ) = \det \big(\mathbf{1}[\chi (j) = j']\big)_{j, j' \in \iota _b} \] be the determinant of the $l \times l$ matrix recording where $\chi $ sends the $\iota _b$-block: the $(j,j')$-entry is $1$ if $\chi (j) = j'$, both read in the $\iota _b$-summand, and $0$ otherwise. Then:

  1. if $\chi = \pi \oplus \rho $ preserves the blocks, then $D(\chi ) = \operatorname {sgn}(\rho )$;

  2. if $\chi $ does not preserve the blocks, then $D(\chi ) = 0$;

  3. consequently, for every commutative ring $R$ and every function $F$ from maps $\iota _a \to \iota _a \sqcup \iota _b$ to $R$,

    \[ \sum _{\chi \in S_{\iota _a \sqcup \iota _b}} \operatorname {sgn}(\chi )\, F\big(\chi |_{\iota _a}\big)\, D(\chi ) \; =\; l! \sum _{\pi \in S_{\iota _a}} \operatorname {sgn}(\pi )\, F(\pi ), \]

    where $\chi |_{\iota _a}$ is the restriction of $\chi $ to the $\iota _a$-summand and, on the right, $\pi $ is read as a map $\iota _a \to \iota _a \sqcup \iota _b$ into the first summand.

Proof

(1) If $\chi = \pi \oplus \rho $, the matrix has $(j,j')$-entry $\mathbf{1}[\rho (j) = j']$; this is the permutation matrix of $\rho $, whose determinant is $\operatorname {sgn}(\rho )$.

(2) A permutation maps the $\iota _a$-summand into itself if and only if it maps the $\iota _b$-summand into itself (the two conditions each say that $\chi $ restricts to a bijection of the finite complement). So if $\chi $ does not preserve the blocks, some $j \in \iota _b$ has $\chi (j)$ in the $\iota _a$-summand; the $j$-th row of the matrix is then identically zero, and the determinant vanishes.

(3) By (2) the sum restricts to the block permutations, which are enumerated bijectively by the pairs $(\pi , \rho ) \in S_{\iota _a} \times S_{\iota _b}$. For $\chi = \pi \oplus \rho $ one has $\chi |_{\iota _a} = \pi $ (as a map into the first summand), $\operatorname {sgn}(\pi \oplus \rho ) = \operatorname {sgn}(\pi )\operatorname {sgn}(\rho )$, and $D(\chi ) = \operatorname {sgn}(\rho )$ by (1); the term is therefore $\operatorname {sgn}(\pi )\operatorname {sgn}(\rho )^2\, F(\pi ) = \operatorname {sgn}(\pi )\, F(\pi )$, independent of $\rho $, and there are $l!$ choices of $\rho $.

□
